    Purport

    There are twelve Ādityas, of which Kṛṣṇa is the principal. Among all the luminaries shining in the sky, the sun is the chief, and in the Brahma-saṁhitā the sun is accepted as the glowing eye of the Supreme Lord. There are fifty varieties of wind blowing in space, and of these winds the controlling deity, Marīci, represents Kṛṣṇa. Among the stars, the moon is the most prominent at night, and thus the moon represents Kṛṣṇa. It appears from this verse that the moon is one of the stars; therefore the stars that twinkle in the sky also reflect the light of the sun. The theory that there are many suns within the universe is not accepted by Vedic literature. The sun is one, and as by the reflection of the sun the moon illuminates, so also do the stars. Since Bhagavad-gītā indicates herein that the moon is one of the stars, the twinkling stars are not suns but are similar to the moon.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    21. Among Ādityas I am Viṣṇu, and among lights, I am the many-rayed sun. Among the winds, I am Marīci. [Note: The story is told in SB 6.18. Indra entered Diti’s womb and cut her son into forty-nine parts. In this way the forty-nine kinds of air known as the Maruts appeared.] I am the moon amidst the stars.
    Commentary

    The genitive case is use for the rest of the chapter to indicate a specific head of group of items and also to indicate a relation to a group. Among the twelve Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu, one of the names of the sun. [Note: The sun is given twelve names according its position in the twelve zodiac signs throughout the year. The names are Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Amśa, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu.] This is My vibhūti. Among all lights, those things which reveal, I am the sun, with a multitude of rays. Marīci is outstanding among the winds.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    21. Among Ādityas I am Viṣṇu, and among lights, I am the many-rayed sun. Among the winds, I am Marīci. [Note: The story is told in SB 6.19. Indra entered Diti’s womb and cut her son into forty-nine parts. In this way the forty-nine kinds of air known as the Maruts appeared.] I am the moon amidst the stars.
    Commentary

    Among the twelve Adityas I am Vāmana (viṣṇu). Among illuminators, I am the sun whose rays spread throughout the universe (aṁśumān-having rays). Among the forty-nine Maruts, I am Marīci. I am the moon, who showers nectar, the lord of the constellations. In these verses the genitive case is used to indicate an outstanding member of a group ( eg. Vāmana among Adityas), and sometimes to indicate a relationship (eg. lord of the constellations).

    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    10.21 Of Adityas, who are twelve in number, I am the twelfth Aditya, called Visnu, who is paramount. Of luminuous bodies, namely, among luminaries in the world, I am the sun, the most brilliant luminary. Of Maruts I am the paramount Marici. Of constellations, I am the moon. The genitive case here is not to specify one out of many included in a group. Its use is the same as what is exemplifed in the statement 'I am the consciousness in all beings' (10.22). I am the moon who is the Lord of the constellations.

Dhata? Mitra? Aryama? Rudra? Varuna? Bhaga? Surya? Vivasvan? Pusham? Savita? Tvashta and Vishnu are the twelve Adityas. The twelve months of the year are the Adityas.The Maruts are the gods controlling the winds. Some hold that there are seven of them while others say there are fortynine.The twelve Adityas? the luminaries like Agni? lightning? etc.? the Maruts? the stars? etc.? are the Samanya Vibhutis (ordinary manifestations) of the Lord. Vishnu? the sun? Marichi? and the moon are His Visesha Vibhutis (special manifestations) and hence they have greater splendour in them.You can superimpose the Lord on the sun and the moon? and meditate on them as forms of the Lord. You can practise the same kind of meditation on all forms mentioned in the following verses of this chapter.

    Personal Guidance
    Of the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; of luminaries I am the radiant sun; of the winds I am Marīci; of stars I am the moon.
    Practical Applications
    • See the sun and moon as Kṛṣṇa's specific opulences, not generic phenomena.
    • Step outside daily and recognize Him.
    • Use sky as reminder.
    Reflection Questions
    • When did I last step outside as remembrance?
    • What sky-experience could become contemplation?
    Analogy

    When a king walks through his treasury, he does not point at every coin. He points at the centerpiece — the great ruby, the largest pearl, the most ancient crown. So Kṛṣṇa, beginning His catalog, names the foremost of each category: Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, the sun among lights, Marīci among the Maruts, the moon among stars.

    Important Words
    • sāma - vedaḥ — the Sāma Veda
      Of the four Vedas, the Sāma is the sung Veda — the one whose verses are not merely recited but melodically chanted. Kṛṣṇa, the divine flutist, picks the musical Veda as His own. The choice is thematically perfect.
    • vāsavaḥ — Indra, the heavenly king
      Indra's title — chief of the Vasus and lord of the deva-realm. In the cosmic administration, this is the top post. Kṛṣṇa claims it as His vibhūti without claiming Indra as Himself in essence.
    • indriyāṇām — of all the senses
      Genitive plural. Among the eleven senses (five jñānendriyas, five karmendriyas, plus manas), Kṛṣṇa picks the mind. The verse establishes the mind's hierarchical seniority over the outer senses.
    • manaḥ — the mind
      The eleventh sense, ruler of the outer ten. Whichever direction the mind turns, the senses follow. Kṛṣṇa's identification with the mind itself is therefore a claim on the controller, not merely the controlled.
    • cetanā — the living force, consciousness
      From cit. Not 'one of many features of a living being' but 'the living-ness itself.' Kṛṣṇa identifies with the very fact-of-being-alive in every creature. The chapter's deepest single claim, made in one word.
    Of the Vedas I am the Sāma Veda; of the demigods I am Indra, the king of heaven; of the senses I am the mind; and in living beings I am the living force [consciousness].

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Each domain is signalled by its musical-vocal apex (Sāma), political apex (Indra), inner organ apex (mind), and ontological apex (consciousness). Kṛṣṇa names what is most representative, not what is most exotic.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Sāma-veda is named for its musicality — Kṛṣṇa identifies with the singing voice of revelation. Vāsava-Indra is the king-archetype. The mind among senses is technical Sāṅkhya — the antaḥkaraṇa coordinator. Cetanā among beings is the very principle of life. Cross-ref Chāndogya 1.1.5 (the udgītha and Sāma) and BG 15.7 (manaḥ ṣaṣṭhānīndriyāṇi).

    Purport

    The difference between matter and spirit is that matter has no consciousness like the living entity; therefore this consciousness is supreme and eternal. Consciousness cannot be produced by a combination of matter.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    22. Among the Vedas, I am the Sāma, and among the devatās, I am Indra. Among the senses, I am the mind. In all living creatures, I am the power of awareness.
    Commentary

    Among the devatās, I am Indra (vāsavaḥ). I am jṣāna-śakti (cetanā) related to all beings. Here the use of the genitive is relational.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    22. Among the Vedas, I am the Sāma, and among the devatās, I am Indra. Among the senses, I am the mind. In all living creatures, I am the power of awareness.
    Commentary

    Among the Vedas, I am the Sāma Veda, because it is outstanding for its sweet songs. Among the devatās I am Indra (vāsavaḥ), their king. Among the senses I am the mind, which inspires the other senses to act and is difficult to conquer. I am the jṣāna śakti or power of consciousness (cetana) belonging to all living entities. This is another case of possessive case meaning relationship rather an outstanding member of a group.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Krsna is explanning 'groups' and He is the most prominent essence of these groups which are easily seen and understood in this material world.

    Personal Guidance
    Of the Vedas I am the Sāma; of demigods I am Indra; of the senses I am the mind; of beings I am consciousness.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize Kṛṣṇa as the consciousness within you.
    • Honor mind as His specific opulence — and yet a tool.
    • Use mental phenomena as remembrance, not just function.
    Reflection Questions
    • How do I treat my own mind — as Him, or as me?
    • What changes with the right attribution?
    Analogy

    A library has many books, but a librarian asked to name the heart of the collection will point to the volume most often opened and most deeply marked. So Kṛṣṇa, among the four Vedas, picks the Sāma — the singing Veda, the chanted one — as His own form. Among all the modes of senses and beings, He picks the mind and the conscious life-force.

    Stories
    Indra and the Vāsava cup

    Indra, the Vāsava-king, holds the cosmic post of administering rain, weather, and battles among the demigods. Kṛṣṇa identifies Himself with Indra here — not because Indra is the supreme but because in the demigod-set, he is the chief.

    Later in Kṛṣṇa's pastimes, when Indra grew proud over the Vraja-pūjā being shifted to Govardhana Hill, Kṛṣṇa would correct him personally. The same Lord who occupies the highest post (vibhūti) also corrects its occupant when ego inflates. Both moves belong to the same Person.

    Important Words
    • rudrāṇām — of all the Rudras
      Genitive plural. The eleven Rudras — destructive deities. Among them, Śaṅkara (Śiva) is chief. Kṛṣṇa's choice tells us where to look in any group: at the head.
    • śaṅkaraḥ — Lord Śiva
      Śiva's name meaning 'maker of auspiciousness.' Even the deity of destruction is named for what he ultimately produces — auspiciousness through dissolution. Kṛṣṇa picks the constructive name.
    • vitta - īśaḥ — the lord of the treasury
      Compound: vitta (wealth) + īśa (lord). Kuvera — head of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, holder of cosmic wealth. The category is wealth-keeping; Kṛṣṇa picks its chief officer.
    • pāvakaḥ — fire
      Agni — among the eight Vasus (gods of light, earth, sky, etc.), Kṛṣṇa picks the purifying fire. The same root pū as pavitram in verse 12. Fire purifies; Kṛṣṇa identifies with the purifier.
    • meruḥ — Mount Meru
      The cosmic axis-mountain, center of the Purāṇic geography. Among all mountains, Meru is supreme — the world-tree's stone counterpart. Kṛṣṇa names the peak that all other peaks are reckoned against.
    Of all the Rudras I am Lord Śiva, of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas I am the Lord of wealth [Kuvera], of the Vasus I am fire [Agni], and of mountains I am Meru.

    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Kṛṣṇa moves through quasi-divine taxa: among the eleven Rudras He is Śiva; among nature-spirit hosts, the wealth-king Kubera; among the eight Vasus, Agni; and among the world-mountains, the cosmic Meru. The pattern targets each class's ruler or paradigmatic specimen.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Identifying with Śaṅkara within the Rudra-set is striking — Vaiṣṇava theology preserves the distinction (Śiva as guṇa-avatāra) while affirming His preeminence in his domain. Meru is the cosmic axis of Purāṇic geography. Pāvaka-Agni is named by the epithet that emphasizes purifying agency. Cross-ref BG 11.6, where the same divine hosts witness the viśva-rūpa.
    Prose order (अन्वय · Anvaya)
    रुद्राणां (मध्ये) शङ्करः च अस्मि; यक्ष-रक्षसां (मध्ये) वित्त-ईशः (अस्मि); वसूनां (मध्ये) पावकः च अस्मि; शिखरिणां (मध्ये) अहं मेरुः (अस्मि) ।

    Purport

    There are eleven Rudras, of whom Śaṅkara, Lord Śiva, is predominant. He is the incarnation of the Supreme Lord in charge of the mode of ignorance in the universe. The leader of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas is Kuvera, the master treasurer of the demigods, and he is a representation of the Supreme Lord. Meru is a mountain famed for its rich natural resources.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    23. Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara [Note: Lord Brahmā said: My dear boy Rudra, you have eleven other names: Manyu, Manu, Mahinasa, Mahān, Śiva, Ṛtadhvaja, Ugraretā, Bhava, Kāla, Vāmadeva and Dhṛtavrata. SB 3.12.12], and among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am Kuvera. [Note: Kuvera is a Yakṣa.] Among the Vasus, I am fire. [Note: The eight Vasus are Āpa, Dhurva, Soma, Dharma, Anila, Pāvaka, Pratyuṣa and Prabhāsa.] Among the peaked mountains, I am Meru.
    Commentary

    Vittesaḥ, lord of wealth, means Kuvera.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    23. Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara [Note: Bhāgavatam says Lord Brahmā said: My dear boy Rudra, you have eleven other names: Manyu, Manu, Mahinasa, Mahān, Śiva, Ṛtadhvaja, Ugraretā, Bhava, Kāla, Vāmadeva and Dhṛtavrata. SB3.12.12], and among the Yakṣas and Rakṣasas, I am Kuvera. [Note: Kuvera is a Yakṣa.] Among the Vasus, I am fire. [Note: The eight Vasus are Āpa, Dhurva, Soma, Dharma, Anila, Pāvaka, Pratyuṣa and Prabhāsa.] Among the peaked mountains, I am Meru.
    Commentary

    Among the eleven Rudras, I am the Rudra named Śaṅkara. I am Kuvera (vitteśaḥ—lord of wealth) the leader of the yakṣas and rakṣasas. Among the eight Vasus, I am Agni (pāvakaḥ). Among high peaks, I am the golden mountain called Meru.

    Commentary

    10.23 रुद्राणाम् among the Rudras? शङ्करः Sankara? च and? अस्मि (I) am? वित्तेशः Kubera? यक्षरक्षसाम्,among celestial fairies and spirits? वसूनाम् among Vasus? पावकः Pavaka? च and? अस्मि (I) am? मेरुः Meru? शिखरिणाम् of mountains? अहम् I.Commentary Rudras are eleven in number. The ten vital airs (Pranas and the UpaPranas? which are five each) and the mind are the eleven Rudras. They are so called because they produce grief when they depart from the body. They have been symbolised in the Puranas as follows Virabhadra? Sankara? Girisa? Ajaikapati? Bhuvanadhisvara? Aherbhujya? Pinaki? Aparajita? Kapali? Sthanu and Bhaga. Among these Rudras? Sankara is regarded as the chief.Vasus are earth? water? fire? air? ether? sun? moon and stars. They are so called because they comprehend the whole universe within them. They have been symbolised in the Puranas as follows Apah? Dhruva? Soma? Dhara? Anila? Anala? Pratyusa and Prabhasa. Of these Anala or Pavaka (fire) is the chief.

Different Puranas give different lists of eleven names.-Tr,] I am Sankara, and among the Yaksas and goblins I am Kubera [God of wealth. Yaksas are a class of demigods who attend on him and guard his wealth.]. Among the Vasus [According to the V.P. they are: Apa, dhruva, Soma, Dharma, Anila, Anala (Fire), Pratyusa and Prabhasa. The Mbh. and the Bh. given a different list.-Tr.] I am Fire, and among the mountains I am Meru.

    Personal Guidance
    Of the Rudras I am Lord Śiva; of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas I am the lord of wealth; of the Vasus I am fire; of mountains I am Meru.
    Practical Applications
    • Don't dismiss other deities; Kṛṣṇa says even they manifest Him.
    • Honor the layered theological richness of the Vedas.
    • Avoid sectarian dismissal.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I been sectarian in dismissing other deities?
    • How does Kṛṣṇa's inclusion of them change my view?
    Analogy

    From the wide world's roster, Kṛṣṇa picks the highest mountain, the chief of the wrath-gods, the lord of wealth, the fire among the Vasus. The principle is steady: in each category, He is the apex. Climb any hierarchy, and at its top He stands; nothing tops Him.

    Stories
    Śiva consoling Pārvatī after Sati

    Lord Śiva, named here as the chief of the eleven Rudras, is famous for both his terrifying form and his soft heart. When Sati immolated herself at Dakṣa's sacrifice, his grief shook the cosmos.

    Kṛṣṇa does not deny Śiva's distinct personhood by saying 'I am Śaṅkara among the Rudras.' He simply claims Śiva as His vibhūti — His chief expansion in the destructive function. The verse confirms what the Bhāgavatam teaches: Śiva is to be honored, but his glory is on loan from the supreme Person.

    Important Words
    • purodhasām — of all priests
      Genitive plural of purodhā — the chief priest who 'stands in front' (puraḥ + dhā). Of all such head-priests, Bṛhaspati is foremost. The verse maps Kṛṣṇa's vibhūti onto the institution of priesthood.
    • bṛhaspatim — Bṛhaspati
      Accusative — 'know Bṛhaspati to be Me.' The guru of the devas. The verse claims that wherever knowledge is being formally transmitted to the highest beings, Kṛṣṇa is the transmitter's transmitter.
    • senānīnām — of all commanders
      Genitive plural of senānī — 'army-leader.' Among military commanders, Skanda (Kārttikeya) is the deva-general. The Mahābhārata's battlefield-listener Arjuna would recognize the choice as flattering and demanding.
    • skandaḥ — Kārttikeya
      The six-headed son of Śiva, commander of the celestial army. Embodies focused martial energy. Kṛṣṇa picks him as the model of the commander — important hearing for the warrior Arjuna.
    • sāgaraḥ — the ocean
      Among all reservoirs of water, the ocean is supreme. Vast, deep, the source from which rivers come and the sink into which they return. A natural metaphor Kṛṣṇa places into His catalog without comment.
    Of priests, O Arjuna, know Me to be the chief, Bṛhaspati. Of generals I am Kārttikeya, and of bodies of water I am the ocean.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Among priests serving kings, Kṛṣṇa is Bṛhaspati — guru of the gods themselves. Among military commanders He is Skanda, Śiva's son and Indra's general. Among reservoirs, the ocean. The verse pairs spiritual authority with martial leadership and cosmic abundance.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Bṛhaspati as devaguru parallels Skanda as devasenāpati — Kṛṣṇa places Himself at the apex of the priestly-martial dyad that structured Indo-Āryan kingship. Sāgara as 'lord of waters' anticipates BG 10.31 (Gaṅgā among rivers). Cross-ref Mahābhārata Vana-parvan stories of Skanda and the Devasenā.

    Purport

    Indra is the chief demigod of the heavenly planets and is known as the king of the heavens. The planet on which he reigns is called Indraloka. Bṛhaspati is Indra’s priest, and since Indra is the chief of all kings, Bṛhaspati is the chief of all priests. And as Indra is the chief of all kings, similarly Skanda, or Kārttikeya, the son of Pārvatī and Lord Śiva, is the chief of all military commanders. And of all bodies of water, the ocean is the greatest. These representations of Kṛṣṇa only give hints of His greatness.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    24. Among head priests, I am the chief one, Bṛhaspati. Among leaders of armies, I am Kārtikeya. Among reservoirs of water, I am the ocean.
    Commentary

    Skanda means Kārtikeya. The form senānīnām is poetic license (the other form would be senāniyam).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    24. Among head priests, I am the chief one, Bṛhaspati. Among leaders of armies, I am Kārtikeya. Among reservoirs of water, I am the ocean.
    Commentary

    Know Me as the chief among Indra’s priests, Bṛhaspati, the master of all. As Indra is the chief among all kings, so his head priest is the chief among all head priests of kings. The form of the word senānīnām as a genitive plural form, with the addition of the “n,” after senānī is poetic license. The normal form would be senānyām. Among all the commanders of kings’ armies, I am Kārttikeya (skandaḥ). Among water bodies (as opposed to rivers), I am the ocean.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The ocean, due to its greatness, neither decreases nor increases. So much water leaves the ocean in the form of evaporation to form the clouds, and so much water enters the ocean in the form of rain and rivers, yet the ocean always remains the same because the ocean's greatness. Krsna in Chapter Two, told Arjuna to be like the ocean, never be agitated by flow of desires that rush to the mind like the ocean is never disturbed although so many rivers rush towards it.

    Personal Guidance
    Of priests I am the chief, Bṛhaspati; of generals I am Skanda; of bodies of water I am the ocean.
    Practical Applications
    • See excellence in any field as Kṛṣṇa's specific opulence.
    • Honor masters in their craft as expressions of Him.
    • Don't separate 'spiritual' from 'excellent.'
    Reflection Questions
    • What master in some field have I underappreciated?
    • How does seeing them as His opulence change my regard?
    Analogy

    In any council a wise host will introduce the head of the priesthood first, then the head of the army, then the largest body of water in the land. So Kṛṣṇa, naming His opulences, takes from each domain its first officer — Bṛhaspati for priests, Skanda for generals, the ocean for waters.

    Stories
    Bṛhaspati teaching the demigods

    Bṛhaspati is the guru of the demigods — their priestly head and counselor. The Mahābhārata records him preceding Indra in council, instructing him in dharma, and defending the celestial order through his prayers.

    Kṛṣṇa names Bṛhaspati not because the priest is the highest being but because in the purodhā-category, he is unmatched. The verse signals to Arjuna: where you see a tradition's primary intellect, recognize a vibhūti of the Lord at work.

    Important Words
    • bhṛguḥ — Bhṛgu
      One of the seven primal sages (sapta-ṛṣi). His descendants include Paraśurāma and many ṛṣi-lineages. Kṛṣṇa picks the sage from whose body so many sage-lines flow — the source-figure within the source-set.
    • ekam akṣaram — the syllable Om (praṇava)
      Compound: ekam (one) + akṣaram (imperishable syllable). Among all sound vibrations (girām), the praṇava is supreme — it contains the Vedas in seed form. The verse honors the syllable that begins every mantra.
    • yajñānām — of sacrifices
      Genitive plural. Of every variety of sacrifice — agnihotra, aśvamedha, rājasūya, jñāna-yajña — Kṛṣṇa picks japa. A radical narrowing: the highest sacrifice is not the most expensive but the most internal.
    • japa - yajñaḥ — the chanting of holy names
      Compound: japa (murmured repetition) + yajña (sacrifice). The verse's most practical line — it tells the householder, the student, the ascetic alike that the door is open through japa. Kali-yuga's central instruction takes its scriptural seat here.
    • himālayaḥ — the Himālayan mountains
      Compound: hima (snow) + ālaya (abode). Among all immovable beings (sthāvara), the Himālayas are supreme — vast, ancient, the source of the Ganges, the home of yogīs. Kṛṣṇa names the great immobile body of the earth itself.
    Of the great sages I am Bhṛgu; of vibrations I am the transcendental oṁ. Of sacrifices I am the chanting of the holy names [japa], and of immovable things I am the Himālayas.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Bhṛgu among sages, Oṁ among utterances, japa among sacrifices, Himālaya among the immovable. The selection privileges the essence over the elaborate — a single syllable, silent repetition, mountain stillness.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Japa-yajña is conspicuously named the supreme sacrifice — more accessible than fire-rituals and inwardly potent. This anticipates the bhakti emphasis: simple sustained chanting is itself the sacrificial summit. Cross-ref Manu 2.85–87, Mahābhārata Śānti-parvan on japa. Oṁ as 'ekam akṣaram' echoes Māṇḍūkya 1 and Kaṭha 1.2.15–17.

    Purport

    Brahmā, the first living creature within the universe, created several sons for the propagation of various kinds of species. Among these sons, Bhṛgu is the most powerful sage. Of all the transcendental vibrations, oṁ ( oṁ-kāra ) represents Kṛṣṇa. Of all sacrifices, the chanting of Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare/ Hare Rāma, Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma, Hare Hare is the purest representation of Kṛṣṇa. Sometimes animal sacrifices are recommended, but in the sacrifice of Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, there is no question of violence. It is the simplest and the purest. Whatever is sublime in the worlds is a representation of Kṛṣṇa. Therefore the Himālayas, the greatest mountains in the world, also represent Him. The mountain named Meru was mentioned in a previous verse, but Meru is sometimes movable, whereas the Himālayas are never movable. Thus the Himālayas are greater than Meru.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas

    Commentary

    Ekākṣara, one syllable, refers to the praṇava om.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    25. Among the great sages, I am Bhṛgu. Among words, I am om. Among sacrifices, I am japa. Among immovable objects, I am the Himālayas.
    Commentary

    Among the great sages, the sons of Brahmā, I am the very powerful Bhṛgu. Among words, I am the single syllable praṇava. Among sacrifices, I am the japa sacrifice, outstanding because it does not involve killing animals. Among immovable, stable objects, I am the Himālayas. Meru and the Himālayas are taken as two separate vibhūtis because the first is outstanding because of height, and the second because of immovability.

    Personal Guidance
    Of the great sages I am Bhṛgu; of vibrations I am the syllable Om; of sacrifices I am japa; of immovable things I am the Himalayas.
    Practical Applications
    • Of all sacrifices, japa is supreme — make it central.
    • Don't undervalue the simplest practice.
    • Cultivate it as the fundamental yajña.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my practice have I sidelined japa?
    • What would centering it restore?
    Analogy

    Among the great sages, the founder of a line; among sounds, the one syllable that carries all; among sacrifices, the simplest and the inwardly fierce — the chanting of holy names. Kṛṣṇa picks not the most elaborate ritual but the one nearest the heart, telling us where He prefers to be found.

    Stories
    Haridāsa Ṭhākura's japa

    Caitanya Mahāprabhu named Haridāsa Ṭhākura nāmācārya — the teacher of the holy name. Haridāsa chanted three hundred thousand names of Hari each day without break, sitting in a cave, beaten by Muslim authorities, never deviating.

    This verse — 'yajñānām japa-yajñaḥ asmi' — is the doctrinal anchor of Haridāsa's life. Among all sacrifices, the silent murmuring of the holy name is supreme, because the Lord Himself dwells in His name. Haridāsa lived this single verse for sixty years.

    Important Words
    • aśvatthaḥ — the banyan tree
      The pippala / aśvattha — sacred to many traditions, central to chapter 15's metaphor of the cosmic tree. Long-lived, multi-trunked, shading. Kṛṣṇa picks the tree whose form will recur as scripture's most extended metaphor.
    • nāradaḥ — Nārada
      The devarṣi — sage among the demigods. Wanderer, vīṇā-player, kīrtana-maker. Kṛṣṇa picks the sage who never sits still, the one whose whole mode of existence is glorification.
    • citrarathaḥ — Citraratha
      Chief of the Gandharvas — celestial musicians. His name means 'one of the wonderful chariot.' Music and motion combined. Kṛṣṇa picks the foremost singer of the heavenly realms.
    • kapilaḥ muniḥ — Kapila Muni
      The avatāra-form of Viṣṇu who taught Sāṅkhya to his mother Devahūti. Note: the Vaiṣṇava Kapila of the Bhāgavatam, not the later atheistic compiler. Kṛṣṇa identifies with the original, devotional Sāṅkhya teacher.
    Of all trees I am the banyan tree, and of the sages among the demigods I am Nārada. Of the Gandharvas I am Citraratha, and among perfected beings I am the sage Kapila.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The chosen tree is the cosmic aśvattha; the chosen divine sage is Nārada the travelling teacher; the chosen Gandharva is Citraratha; the chosen siddha is Kapila — founder of Sāṅkhya. Each pick is iconic of its class.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Aśvattha returns explicitly in BG 15.1 as the symbol of saṁsāra. Nārada will reappear named in 10.13 (already invoked) and at 11.37. Kapila here is the divine ṛṣi-author of Sāṅkhya — Vaiṣṇava tradition identifies him as Kṛṣṇa's own avatāra (Bhāgavatam 3.24). Cross-ref BG 2.39 where Sāṅkhya was already named as a precursor system.

    Purport

    The banyan tree ( aśvattha ) is one of the highest and most beautiful trees, and people in India often worship it as one of their daily morning rituals. Amongst the demigods they also worship Nārada, who is considered the greatest devotee in the universe. Thus he is the representation of Kṛṣṇa as a devotee. The Gandharva planet is filled with entities who sing beautifully, and among them the best singer is Citraratha. Amongst the perfect living entities, Kapila, the son of Devahūti, is a representative of Kṛṣṇa. He is considered an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, and His philosophy is mentioned in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. Later on another Kapila became famous, but his philosophy was atheistic. Thus there is a gulf of difference between them.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    26. Among the trees, I am the pippala. [Note: This tree is regards as a representative of Viṣṇu.] Among the divine sages, I am Nārada. Among the Gandharvas, I am Citraratha. Among perfected beings, I am Kapila.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    26. Among the trees, I am the pippala. [Note: This tree is regards as a representative of Viṣṇu.] Among the divine sages, I am Nārada. Among the gandharvas, I am Citraratha. Among perfected beings, I am Kapila.
    Commentary

    Among all trees worthy of worship, I am the excellent pippala tree. Among divine sages, I am Narada, outstanding because of his outstanding level of bhakti. Among Gandharvas, I am Citraratha, outstanding because of his excellent singing ability. Among the Siddhas, who have natural mystic powers like becoming small, I am the muni Kapila, son of Kardama.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    'Nara' means God and 'ada' means 'giver'. Narada is called like that because he gives God to everyone.

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    Nāra means “mankind” or “spiritual.” Da means “giving or granting.” Nārada, who has disciples all

    over the universe, gives God to everyone.

    Citraratha was Arjuna’s friend, and he taught Arjuna the art of singing.

    Personal Guidance
    Of trees I am the banyan; of demigod sages I am Nārada; of Gandharvas I am Citraratha; of perfected beings I am Kapila.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor Nārada Muni as the model of the wandering devotee.
    • Read Nārada's pastimes regularly.
    • Receive Bhakti-sūtra-style teachings as Kṛṣṇa-direct.
    Reflection Questions
    • What model of devotee-life calls me?
    • Whose example am I underusing?
    Analogy

    Among trees, the long-lived banyan whose aerial roots become new trunks; among devarṣis, the wandering Nārada who carries Kṛṣṇa's name from world to world; among Gandharvas, the celestial musician; among the perfected, the sage who taught his own mother. Kṛṣṇa picks the spreaders — those who do not stay in one shape or one place.

    Stories
    Nārada in his previous life

    In a previous life Nārada was the son of a maidservant who served visiting Vaiṣṇavas. Eating their remnants, hearing their kīrtana, he received a single seed of bhakti. When his mother died, he wandered into the forest and there had direct darśana of the Lord — once, briefly.

    From that single touch he became the wandering preacher of three worlds, named here as the chief among devarṣis. The Bhāgavatam (canto 1) records the story so the reader understands why Kṛṣṇa names Nārada — not for cosmic status but for the constancy of his mission of spreading Hari-kathā.

    Kapila instructing Devahūti

    Kapila Muni, named here as the chief of the perfected (siddhas), was born to Devahūti as her son. When Devahūti at the right age asked for spiritual instruction, Kapila — though her son — became her guru. The Bhāgavatam preserves the entire transmission.

    Kṛṣṇa picks Kapila as His siddha-vibhūti because the perfection here is not magical power but the perfection of teaching one's own kin into liberation. The choice tells us what siddhi truly means in Kṛṣṇa's reckoning.

    Important Words
    • uccaiḥśravasam — Uccaiḥśravā
      The divine seven-headed horse, white as a conch, produced from the milk ocean's churning. Among aśvas, the very type. Kṛṣṇa picks the original from which the form descends.
    • amṛta - udbhavam — produced from the churning of the ocean for nectar
      Compound: amṛta (nectar) + udbhavam (arisen from). The horse's origin story is built into his epithet. The verse honors the manthana-pastime by referencing it within the catalog.
    • airāvatam — Airāvata
      The four-tusked white elephant who became Indra's mount. Among gaja-indras (lordly elephants), the supreme. Kṛṣṇa picks the mount of the chief demigod — a vibhūti within a vibhūti.
    • nara - adhipam — the king, the chief of men
      Compound: nara (man) + adhipa (overlord). Among humans, the lawful king is Kṛṣṇa's vibhūti. The verse legitimates monarchy as a sacred function when properly held — relevant for Arjuna, who was fighting precisely to restore lawful kingship.
    Of horses know Me to be Uccaiḥśravā, produced during the churning of the ocean for nectar. Of lordly elephants I am Airāvata, and among men I am the monarch.

    Three regal selections: Uccaiḥśravas the celestial horse from the nectar-churning, Airāvata Indra's white elephant, and among men the sovereign. The motif is 'first-of-kind won from divine effort.'

    Uccaiḥśravas and Airāvata are both ratnas of the samudra-manthana — Kṛṣṇa highlights items emergent from cooperative cosmic effort, hinting that opulence has a producing context.     Purport

    The devotee demigods and the demons ( asuras ) once took part in churning the sea. From this churning, nectar and poison were produced, and Lord Śiva drank the poison. From the nectar were produced many entities, of which there was a horse named Uccaiḥśravā. Another animal produced from the nectar was an elephant named Airāvata. Because these two animals were produced from nectar, they have special significance, and they are representatives of Kṛṣṇa. Amongst the human beings, the king is the representative of Kṛṣṇa because Kṛṣṇa is the maintainer of the universe, and the kings, who are appointed on account of their godly qualifications, are maintainers of their kingdoms. Kings like Mahārāja Yudhiṣṭhira, Mahārāja Parīkṣit and Lord Rāma were all highly righteous kings who always thought of the citizens’ welfare. In Vedic literature, the king is considered to be the representative of God. In this age, however, with the corruption of the principles of religion, monarchy decayed and is now finally abolished. It is to be understood that in the past, however, people were more happy under righteous kings.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

    Commentary

    Among horses I am Ucchaiḥśrava. Among elephants know that I am Airāvata. The special quality of both of these is that they arose from the churning of the milk ocean for the purpose of gaining nectar. [Note: Both became the property of Indra. Ucchaiḥśravas means “loudly praised.” Airāvata is so called because his mother was named Irāvatī.] I am the king (narādhipam) among men, who is fixed in dharma and has unbearable strength.

    Personal Guidance
    Of horses I am Uccaiḥśravas, born of nectar; of elephants Airāvata; of men, the king.
    Practical Applications
    • See magnificence in beings as His expression.
    • Honor leadership as His specific opulence.
    • Don't be cynical about kingly authority — it can be His.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I been cynical about authority that may be Him?
    • How does this verse temper that cynicism?
    Analogy

    The horse born from the milk-ocean's churning, the elephant who carries Indra, the human who governs nations — Kṛṣṇa picks from each species not the ordinary specimen but the one whose origin is mythic and whose function is rulership. Where dominion stands, His vibhūti stands.

    Stories
    The churning of the milk ocean

    When the demigods and demons together churned the milk ocean (samudra-manthana) to obtain the nectar of immortality, fourteen jewels emerged before the amṛta-kalaśa itself. Among them were Uccaiḥśravā the divine horse and Airāvata the lordly elephant.

    The Bhāgavatam's eighth canto records the whole episode. Kṛṣṇa names two of those churning-born jewels here — fitting, because the same Lord, in His Kūrma form, supported Mount Mandara beneath the ocean during that very churning. The animals He picks were lifted into being by His own pastime.

    Important Words
    • vajram — the thunderbolt
      Indra's weapon, made from Dadhīci's bones (see above). Among all weapons, the most charged — physically and ethically. Kṛṣṇa picks the one whose existence already required ultimate sacrifice.
    • kāma - dhuk — the surabhi cow, the wish-fulfilling cow
      Compound: kāma (desire) + dhuk (yielding, milking). The cow who supplies whatever one wishes for. Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd, picks the highest cow — fittingly tying His vibhūti to His own beloved animal.
    • kandarpaḥ — Cupid, the god of love
      Among causes of procreation (prajanaḥ), Kandarpa — the deity of erotic desire — is supreme. Note the qualifier in many commentaries: the dharmic kāma, the one that serves prajā, not the rogue passion. Kṛṣṇa claims the regulated, generative force.
    • vāsukiḥ — Vāsuki
      Among serpents (sarpāḥ — venomous ones), Vāsuki is king. He served as the churning-rope around Mount Mandara during the milk-ocean churning. Kṛṣṇa identifies with the serpent-king who once participated in His own Kūrma pastime.
    Of weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows I am the surabhi. Of causes for procreation I am Kandarpa, the god of love, and of serpents I am Vāsuki.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Vajra among weapons (Indra's bolt), Kāmadhuk among cows, Kandarpa as the lawful drive of procreation, Vāsuki among serpents. Even sexuality, properly aligned with regeneration, is named as a divine vibhūti.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The Gītā here legitimizes lawful procreative desire (prajanaḥ kandarpaḥ) as itself a manifestation of the Lord — distinct from the lust condemned at 3.37 and 16.21. Vāsuki's later role at the manthana is implicit. The selection criterion alternates between symbol of power (vajra), of yielding abundance (kāmadhuk), and of sovereign instance (Vāsuki).

    Purport

    The thunderbolt, indeed a mighty weapon, represents Kṛṣṇa’s power. In Kṛṣṇaloka in the spiritual sky there are cows which can be milked at any time, and they give as much milk as one likes. Of course such cows do not exist in this material world, but there is mention of them in Kṛṣṇaloka. The Lord keeps many such cows, which are called surabhi. It is stated that the Lord is engaged in herding the surabhi cows. Kandarpa is the sex desire for presenting good sons; therefore Kandarpa is the representative of Kṛṣṇa. Sometimes sex is engaged in only for sense gratification; such sex does not represent Kṛṣṇa. But sex for the generation of good children is called Kandarpa and represents Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    28. Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt. Among cows, I am the Kāmadhenu. Among types of lust, I am that for producing offspring. Among snakes, I am Vāsuki.
    Commentary

    Among the cows, I am Kāmadhenu (kāma-dhuk). [Note: This cow was born from the churning of the milk ocean. She gives unlimited milk.] Among the types of lust, I am lust for the purpose of producing offspring (prajanaḥ).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    28. Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt. Among cows, I am the Kāmadhenu. Among types of lust, I am that for producing offspring. Among snakes, I am Vāsuki.
    Commentary

    Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt. I am the kāma dhenu, who fulfills whatever one desires, among the cows. I am that lust which produces children (prajanaḥ). Ca here indicates that I am not lust whose only purpose is pleasure of the sex act. Among snakes with one head, I am Vāsuki.

    Personal Guidance
    Of weapons I am the thunderbolt; of cows the surabhi; of progenitors I am Kandarpa; of serpents I am Vāsuki.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor the cow as His opulence — protect, don't exploit.
    • Recognize even procreative force as His expression when in dharma.
    • Don't reduce nature to commodity.
    Reflection Questions
    • How do I relate to cows in my food and product choices?
    • What change is being asked?
    Analogy

    From weapons, the thunderbolt that gods themselves use; from cows, the wish-fulfilling surabhi; from procreative force, the god of love himself; from serpents, the king of nāgas. Kṛṣṇa picks the apex of each natural power — and one of them is the desire that drives families into being. Even kāma, lawfully placed, is His vibhūti.

    Stories
    Vajra forged from Dadhīci's bones

    When the demon Vṛtra terrorized the demigods, no ordinary weapon could pierce him. The sage Dadhīci, on Indra's request, gave up his own body so that his bones could be forged into the vajra — the thunderbolt named here.

    The Bhāgavatam (canto 6) records the story in detail. Kṛṣṇa picks the vajra as His weapon-vibhūti because behind that thunderbolt lies a sage's complete self-offering. The weapon's supremacy comes from the giver's surrender.

    Important Words
    • anantaḥ — Ananta
      'Endless.' The thousand-hooded serpent on whose coils Viṣṇu reclines in the causal ocean. Among the many-hooded nāgas, He is supreme. Note also: Ananta is Saṅkarṣaṇa, a direct expansion of the Lord — vibhūti within a personal expansion.
    • varuṇaḥ — the demigod controlling the water
      Lord of all aquatics (yādasām). Ancient deity of cosmic waters and oaths. Kṛṣṇa picks the deva who governs both the literal seas and the moral element of pledged truth.
    • aryamā — Aryamā
      Chief of the ancestors (pitṛs). The deity who receives ancestral offerings. Kṛṣṇa identifies with the head of the world of the departed — a category most living beings would prefer not to think about.
    • yamaḥ — the controller of death
      Yamarāja — among saṁyamatām (regulators, restrainers), the supreme. Death itself, given a face and a function. Kṛṣṇa puts the Lord of the dead inside His vibhūti catalog, neutralizing the fear that fact-of-death normally produces.
    Of the many-hooded Nāgas I am Ananta, and among the aquatics I am the demigod Varuṇa. Of departed ancestors I am Aryamā, and among the dispensers of law I am Yama, the lord of death.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Two cosmic snakes are distinguished (sarpa vs. nāga); among the divine ones Kṛṣṇa is Ananta-Śeṣa, the bed of Viṣṇu. Among ocean-dwellers, Varuṇa the lawful king. Among ancestors, Aryaman the chief pitṛ. Among restrainers, Yama, the just.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The distinction between sarpa (10.28) and nāga (10.29) is a Purāṇic convention: sarpa is ordinary, nāga is divine. Ananta as the limitless serpent-base of cosmic order echoes Kṛṣṇa's own anantatā (10.19, 10.40). The choice of Yama 'among restrainers' subtly nominates death itself as a divine regulator — to be repeated in 10.34.

    Purport

    Among the many-hooded Nāga serpents, Ananta is the greatest, as is the demigod Varuṇa among the aquatics. They both represent Kṛṣṇa. There is also a planet of Pitās, ancestors, presided over by Aryamā, who represents Kṛṣṇa. There are many living entities who give punishment to the miscreants, and among them Yama is the chief. Yama is situated in a planet near this earthly planet. After death those who are very sinful are taken there, and Yama arranges different kinds of punishments for them.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    29. Among Nāgas, [Note: Nāgas have many heads, whereas sarpas, regular snakes, have only one head each.] I am Ananta. Among inhabitants of water I am Varuṇa. Among the Pitṛs, I am Aryamā. Among punishers, I am Yama.
    Commentary

    Among the inhabitants of the water (yādasām), I am Varuṇa. Among those who punish (saṁyamatām), I am Yama.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    29. Among Nāgas, I am Ananta. Among inhabitants of water, I am Varuṇa. Among the pitṛas, I am Aryamā. Among punishers, I am Yama.
    Commentary

    Among the Nāgas with many heads, I am Śeṣa. Among aquatic inhabitants, I am Varuṇa, their leader. Among the Pitṛs, I am the lord of the pitṛs called Aryamā. Among punishers, I am Yama who gives just punishment. Using saṁyamatām instead of the regular form saṁyacchatām is poetic license.

    Personal Guidance
    Of Nāgas I am Ananta; of aquatics I am Varuṇa; of ancestors I am Aryamā; of dispensers of law I am Yama.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor Yama (Lord of death) — He brings dharma's accountability.
    • Treat dharmic discipline as Kṛṣṇa's specific opulence.
    • Don't fear death; it serves dharma.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I been resisting accountability?
    • What does Yama's dharma require of me?
    Analogy

    The thousand-hooded eternal Ananta on whose coils Viṣṇu reclines; the lord of waters; the chief of ancestors; the regulator of all who must die. Kṛṣṇa picks the figures who hold the unseen orders together — beneath, in the depths, behind death's curtain. The visible world rests on these less-visible kings.

    Stories
    Yama and Naciketas

    When the boy Naciketas was sent to Yama's house and waited three days without food, Yama returned and offered him three boons. The third was the most dangerous: tell me what lies beyond death.

    Yama tried to deflect, offered wealth, sons, kingdoms — Naciketas refused them all. Yama then taught the Self that does not die, the famous core of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad. Kṛṣṇa names Yama here as His vibhūti among regulators — and Yama's own greatest moment was teaching the Self that exceeds his jurisdiction.

    Important Words
    • prahlādaḥ — Prahlāda
      The demon-prince who is the supreme devotee. Kṛṣṇa picks him as the daitya-vibhūti — radical inversion: the highest demon, by Kṛṣṇa's reckoning, is the one who is not really demonic at all. The category is redefined by the choice.
    • kālaḥ — time
      Among kalayatām — subduers, the ones who bring down. Time is the supreme subduer; it brings down empires, ages, demigods. Kṛṣṇa identifies with the impersonal force that even gods cannot resist.
    • mṛga - indraḥ — the lion
      Compound: mṛga (animal) + indra (king). The lion as king of beasts. Note: also a name for Nṛsiṁhadeva — the man-lion who killed Hiraṇyakaśipu. The verse's previous Prahlāda-name and this lion-name resonate.
    • vainateyaḥ — Garuḍa, son of Vinatā
      Garuḍa identified by his mother's name — the standard patronymic-style for him. As Viṣṇu's eternal carrier, he is the chief of birds. Kṛṣṇa's avian vibhūti is the servant-bird, not the most powerful raptor.
    Among the Daitya demons I am the devoted Prahlāda, among subduers I am time, among beasts I am the lion, and among birds I am Garuḍa.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Among the demonic Daitya lineage Kṛṣṇa picks the devotee — Prahlāda — not the conqueror. Among reckoners-of-things, He is Time itself. Lion among beasts, Garuḍa among birds. Devotion can shine even in a hostile lineage.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Naming Prahlāda inside the daitya category is a deliberate scandal: the Lord's vibhūti among demons is the demon-prince who refused to be a demon. This deeply foreshadows the doctrine of unconditional bhakti and prefigures Nṛsiṁha-līlā (Bhāgavatam 7). 'Kālaḥ kalayatām' is famously echoed in BG 11.32 (kālo'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt).

    Purport

    Diti and Aditi are two sisters. The sons of Aditi are called Ādityas, and the sons of Diti are called Daityas. All the Ādityas are devotees of the Lord, and all the Daityas are atheistic. Although Prahlāda was born in the family of the Daityas, he was a great devotee from his childhood. Because of his devotional service and godly nature, he is considered to be a representative of Kṛṣṇa. There are many subduing principles, but time wears down all things in the material universe and so represents Kṛṣṇa. Of the many animals, the lion is the most powerful and ferocious, and of the million varieties of birds, Garuḍa, the bearer of Lord Viṣṇu, is the greatest.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas

    Translation
    30. Among the demons, I am Prahlāda. Among controllers, I am time. Among animals, I am the lion. Among birds, I am Garuḍa.
    Commentary

    Among subjugators (kalayatām), I am time. Among animals, I am the lion (mṛgendraḥ). Among birds, I am Garuḍa (vainateyaḥ).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    30. Among the daityas, I am Prahlāda. Among controllers, I am time. Among animals, I am the lion. Among birds, I am Garuḍa.
    Commentary

    Among the descendents of Diti, called the daityas, I am their leader, Prahlāda, the best because of his intense faith in the Lord. Among those things that control, I am time. Among animals, I am the lion, outstanding because of its courage. Among birds, I am Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, the best because he is the carrier of Viṣṇu. [Note: Viṣṇu, pleased with Garuḍa after he exhibited prowess in stealing the pot of nectar, asked him to take a boon. Garuḍa asked to be His carrier and be immortal without drinking nectar. Viṣṇu granted both requests.]

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Why 'time'? Because time controls everything.

    Personal Guidance
    Of the demoniac I am Prahlāda; of subduers I am time; of beasts I am the lion; of birds Garuḍa.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize Prahlāda as a demoniac descendant who is supreme devotee.
    • Trust that lineage doesn't determine devotion.
    • Apply this to any 'wrong family' you may feel born into.
    Reflection Questions
    • What inherited shadow do I assume blocks devotion?
    • How does Prahlāda's example free me?
    Analogy

    Of all demons, the one who refused to hate the Lord; of all subduers, time itself, which subdues even kings; of all beasts, the lion; of all birds, the carrier of Viṣṇu. Kṛṣṇa picks one demon — and it is the demon who turned. Even within the asura-class, His vibhūti is the bhakta within it.

    Stories
    Prahlāda's protection

    Born to Hiraṇyakaśipu — the chief demon of the universe — Prahlāda was supposed to inherit his father's hatred of Viṣṇu. Instead, instructed in the womb by Nārada, he emerged a devotee. His father tried fire, poison, serpents, mountains, weapons; nothing worked.

    When Nṛsiṁhadeva finally tore Hiraṇyakaśipu apart, the avatāra's fierceness subsided only at Prahlāda's touch. The Bhāgavatam (canto 7) records the entire episode. Kṛṣṇa names Prahlāda specifically — not Hiraṇyakaśipu, the famous demon-king — because in any category Kṛṣṇa picks His devotee, not the category's most powerful occupant.

    Garuḍa carrying the Lord

    Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, named here as the chief among birds, became Viṣṇu's eternal mount through his own austerity. He once stole the nectar from Indra to free his mother from slavery — yet, despite his power to challenge demigods, he chose service over independent glory.

    The verse picks Garuḍa not for his strength but for his function. Among all birds, the supreme is the one who carries the Lord. Kṛṣṇa's vibhūti is wherever service is fully tendered.

    Important Words
    • pavanaḥ — the wind
      From the root pū — 'to purify.' The wind purifies by moving — clearing air, carrying away staleness. Kṛṣṇa picks the natural purifier-in-motion as the chief of purifying agents.
    • rāmaḥ — Rāma
      Among śastra-bhṛts (weapon-bearers), Rāma is supreme. The avatāra-king who killed Rāvaṇa with the bow. Kṛṣṇa names His own previous-yuga form here — a subtle internal cross-reference.
    • makaraḥ — the shark, the great sea-creature
      Among jhaṣāḥ (fish, aquatic creatures), the makara is the largest, the predator who rules the depths. Also the vehicle of Varuṇa and the symbol on Kandarpa's banner. Kṛṣṇa picks the apex of the aquatic order.
    • jāhnavī — the river Ganges
      Named for the sage Jahnu, who once drank her and released her from his ear. Among rivers, the supreme — purifier of the dead, descended by Bhagīratha's austerity. Kṛṣṇa's river-vibhūti is the river that washes karmic load.
    Of purifiers I am the wind, of the wielders of weapons I am Rāma, of fishes I am the shark, and of flowing rivers I am the Ganges.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Wind among purifiers, Rāma among weapon-bearers, makara among fishes, Gaṅgā among rivers. Kṛṣṇa picks instances of irresistible motion and sanctifying flow — purifying air and sacred water flank martial perfection.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Rāma here is Dāśarathi Rāma, the warrior-king of Ayodhyā. Jāhnavī (Gaṅgā) is named via the patronymic from Jahnu, evoking the descent-myth (gaṅgāvataraṇa). The Makara is both fish-lord and Varuṇa's mount. Together these four highlight the divine inside flowing, cleansing, and decisively acting agencies — cross-ref BG 11.39 (vāyur yamo'gniḥ).

    Purport

    Of all the aquatics the shark is one of the biggest and is certainly the most dangerous to man. Thus the shark represents Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    31. Among purifiers and the swift, I am the wind. Among holders of weapons, I am Paraśurāma. Among the fishes, I am the makara. Among rivers, I am the Gaṅgā.
    Commentary

    Of moving or purifying agents, I am the wind. Among bearers of weapons, I am Paraśurāma. He is suitable as a vibhūti because He is an aveśāvatāra, and because He is an outstanding jīva among those who have been given powers by the Lord. [Note: Rāma is taken as Paraśurāma rather than Rāmacandra, since he is a jīva . A jīva can be a vibhūti, but not the Lord Himself.] Padma Purāṇa, quoted in Bhagavatāmṛta says “O devi, I have recited to you the story of Paraśurāma, a śaktyaveśa avatāra of the Lord.” Also it says, “He took birth as an empowered jīva.” The characteristics of the aveśāvatāra are also mentioned in the Bhagavatāmṛta. “Where a jīva is filled with portions of jṣāna-śakti or other śakti of the Lord, he is called aveśāvatāra.” (Laghu Bhagavatāmṛta 1.4 .39, 1.4.38, 1.1.18) Among fish (jhaṣāṇām), I am the makara, a special type of fish. Among rivers (srotasām), I am the Gaṅgā.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    31. Among purifiers and the swift, I am the wind. Among holders of weapons, I am Paraśurāma. Among the fishes, I am the makara. Among rivers, I am the Gaṅgā.
    Commentary

    Among purifiers or among swift things, I am the wind. I am Paraśurāma (rāmaḥ) among wielders of weapons. Among fish I am the makara, a special variety of fish. Among flowing waters, I am the Gaṅgā.

    Personal Guidance
    Of purifiers I am the wind; of warriors I am Rāma; of fishes I am the shark; of flowing rivers I am the Ganges.
    Practical Applications
    • Bathe in or remember the Ganges as a purification practice.
    • Honor Rāma as warrior-Lord, not just gentle prince.
    • Recognize the wind, rivers, and creatures as specific Kṛṣṇa-presences.
    Reflection Questions
    • When did I last connect with sacred water?
    • What practice could renew that?
    Analogy

    Among purifiers, the wind that carries fragrance and clears stagnation; among warriors, the avatāra who teaches dharma with the bow; among fish, the predator who masters the depths; among rivers, the one whose touch washes lifetimes. Kṛṣṇa picks the agents that move, cleanse, and carry across.

    Stories
    Rāma's vow of one word, one wife, one arrow

    Rāma, named here as the chief among wielders of weapons, was renowned not only for his archery but for his single-pointed dharma. One word given was kept; one wife alone was married; one arrow drawn was enough.

    When Rāvaṇa abducted Sītā, Rāma did not unleash mass destruction — he assembled an army of monkeys, observed every protocol of war, and finally killed Rāvaṇa with one well-placed shaft. Kṛṣṇa names Rāma as His weapon-bearer-vibhūti because among śastra-bhṛts, none combined skill and restraint so completely.

    Bhagīratha bringing the Ganges

    King Bhagīratha did austerities for years so that the heavenly Ganges would descend and purify his ancestors' ashes. Ganges agreed but warned her fall would shatter the earth. Śiva caught her in his hair; she emerged as a softer stream and reached the plains.

    Kṛṣṇa names her here as His river-vibhūti — Jāhnavī, named for the sage Jahnu who later swallowed and re-released her. The whole story is one of purification through cosmic cooperation. The verse's word pavatām — 'of purifiers' — applies equally to the wind (named in this verse) and to her.

    Important Words
    • sargāṇām — of all creations
      Genitive plural of sarga — 'emanation, creation.' Echoes verse 20's ādiḥ-madhyam-antaḥ — but applied now to the cosmos at large rather than to individual beings. Kṛṣṇa is the bookends and the spine of every creative cycle.
    • adhyātma - vidyā — spiritual knowledge
      Compound: adhyātma (concerning the self) + vidyā (knowledge). Of all branches of vidyā — grammar, logic, astronomy, statecraft — Kṛṣṇa picks the one that asks who is doing the knowing. The verse establishes ranks among knowledges.
    • vidyānām — of all education
      Genitive plural of vidyā. The verse's framing: among the many knowledges humans pursue, one is supreme. Kṛṣṇa hierarchizes learning itself.
    • vādaḥ — the natural conclusion
      From vad — 'to speak.' Of three modes of debate (vāda — truth-seeking discussion; jalpa — argument for victory; vitaṇḍā — destructive cavil), vāda is the highest. Kṛṣṇa identifies only with truth-seeking discourse, not with adversarial wrangling.
    • pravadatām — of arguments, of debaters
      Present participle, genitive plural — 'of those who argue.' Among debaters, Kṛṣṇa is the conclusive position itself, not any particular debater. The verse claims the conclusion of every right argument as His vibhūti.
    Of all creations I am the beginning and the end and also the middle, O Arjuna. Of all sciences I am the spiritual science of the self, and among logicians I am the conclusive truth.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Among created things Kṛṣṇa is the alpha, omega, and middle. Among sciences, the science of the Self. Among debate-styles, the vāda — the truth-seeking dialogue (not jalpa or vitaṇḍā).
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The nyāya tradition distinguishes three modes of disputation: vāda (cooperative truth-seeking), jalpa (winning-debate), vitaṇḍā (refutation-only). By identifying with vāda, Kṛṣṇa underwrites philosophy-as-shared-inquiry over polemics. Adhyātma-vidyā as queen of sciences echoes BG 9.2 (rāja-vidyā rāja-guhyaṁ).

    Purport

    Among the created manifestations, the first is the creation of the total material elements. As explained before, the cosmic manifestation is created and conducted by Mahā-viṣṇu, Garbhodaka-śāyī Viṣṇu and Kṣīrodaka-śāyī Viṣṇu, and then again it is annihilated by Lord Śiva. Brahmā is a secondary creator. All these agents of creation, maintenance and annihilation are incarnations of the material qualities of the Supreme Lord. Therefore He is the beginning, the middle and the end of all creation. For advanced education there are various kinds of books of knowledge, such as the four Vedas, their six supplements, the Vedānta-sūtra, books of logic, books of religiosity and the Purāṇas. So all together there are fourteen divisions of books of education. Of these, the book which presents adhyātma-vidyā, spiritual knowledge – in particular, the Vedānta-sūtra – represents Kṛṣṇa. Among logicians there are different kinds of argument. Supporting one’s argument with evidence that also supports the opposing side is called jalpa. Merely trying to defeat one’s opponent is called vitaṇḍā. But the actual conclusion is called vāda. This conclusive truth is a representation of Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    32. I am the creation, destruction and maintenance of all elements. Among types of knowledge, I am knowledge of the soul. Among types of debate I am vāda.
    Commentary

    I am the creation (adiḥ) and destruction (antaḥ) of ether and other elements (sargāṇām), and the maintenance of them as well. One should meditate upon creation, maintenance and destruction as My vibhūtis. This means that I, the Supreme Lord, am the creator, maintainer and destroyer. Among types of knowledge, I am knowledge of the self. Among types of argumentation in order to establish ones own idea and defeat others ideas, such as jalpa and vitaṇḍa, I am vāda, which attempts to discern actual truth with the goal of coming to a conclusion. [Note: Vāda, jalpa and vitaṇḍa are famous as the three types of argument. When both parties desire to win by establishing their own opinion with proofs and arguments, and refuting the opponent’s view with circumvention (chala), false generalization (jāti) and syllogistic fault (nigraha-sthāna), it is called jalpa. When one party refutes the opponent’s view (by the above means), without establishing his own opinion, it is called vitaṇḍa. These two types of debate, with a desire to win, simply display skill in debating and bear no result. That discussion having a desire for truth is called vāda.]

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    32. I am the creation, destruction and maintenance of all elements. Among types of knowledge, I am knowledge of the soul. Among types of debate, I am vāda.
    Commentary

    Among the things created out of matter, starting from mahat tattva, I am the beginning, the end and the middle. Their creation, maintenance and destruction should be thought of being My vibhūtis. In verse 20 Kṛṣṇa said aham ādiś ca madhyaṁ ca bhūtānām anta eva ca. His vibhūtis of creation, maintenance and destruction were in reference to the living entities, His conscious parts, in that verse. Thus there is no repetition in the present verse, since this refers to the material elements. aṅgāni vedāś catvāro mīmāṁsā nyāya-vistaraḥ dharma-śāstraṁ purāṇaṁ ca vidyā hy etāś caturdaśa The four Vedas with its six aṅgas, [Note: Sikṣa (pronunciation), chanda (meter), vyākaraṇa (grammar), nirukta (meaning), jyotiṣa (astrology), and kalpa (ritual)are the six vedāṅgas.] mīmāṁsā, nyāya, [Note: It is unclear what these are nyāya can refer to Brahma Sūtras, or Gautama’s Nyāya, or logic in general. Mīmāṁsā can refer to karma mīmāṁsā doctrine.] dharma śastra, and purāṇas are considered the fourteen types of knowledge. Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6.28 Among these types of knowledge, I am the knowledge concerning ātmā, the knowledge of Vedānta with four chapters (catur lakṣāṇī vidyā) which defines paramātmā and His associates. [Note: The first chapter of Vedānta shows Brahman as the subject of the Vedas. The second chapter solves all contradictions with other scriptures. The third chapter deals with sādhana for attaining Brahman. The fourth chapter describes the attainment of Brahman.] I am vāda of those who debate. Vāda, jalpa and vitaṇḍa are famous as the three types of argument. When both parties desire to win by establishing their own opinion with proofs and arguments, and refuting the opponent’s view with circumvention (chala), false generalization (jāti) and syllogistic fault (nigraha sthāna), it is called jalpa. When one party refutes the opponent’s view (by the above means), without establishing his own opinion, it is called vitaṇḍa. These two types of debate, with a desire to win, simply display skill in debating and bear no result. That discussion having a desire for truth is called vāda. Being outstanding for being fruitful in determining truth, vāda is My vibhūti.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In text 20, Krsna also said: "I am the beginning, the middle and the end of all beings (sentient beings)." Here He refers to non‑sentient beings. In 'nyaya', or logic, there are different types of ways to get the truth. They are called: 'vitendra', 'vada', and 'jalpa'. Krsna here says: "I am vada, the natural conclusion." The difference is: 'vitendra' is when someone is arguing just concerned to defeat the other party, not really very concerned to find the truth. 'Jalpa' means that one wants to proof that he is correct and the others are wrong, regardless of who is actually correct. In 'vada' one wants to find out what the actual truth is by using argument and discussion to do that.

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    In Text 20, Kṛṣṇa said He was the beginning, middle and end of all beings. Śrīla Baladeva Vidyāb-

    hūṣaṇa says that in that verse He was referring to all sentient beings. Here, however, Kṛṣṇa says

    that He is also the beginning, middle and end of every nonsentient creation.

    Nyāya, logic, teaches various ways to reach a conclusion, including vitaṇḥā, vāda and jalpa. Kṛṣṇa

    says, “I am vāda, the natural conclusion.” Vāda is debate carried out fairly according to standard

    rules, without trying to force the establishment of a particular conclusion. Vitaṇḥā is quibbling, or

    merely destructive argument in which one tries to defeat the opponent by any means possible, but

    does nothing substantial to positively prove one’s own thesis. Jalpa, using various deceptive means

    to fool the opposition, is unfair argument. Vitaṇḥā and jalpa are forms of argument in which win-

    ning, not necessarily determining the truth, is the main consideration.

    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    10.32 O Arjuna sarganam, of creations; I am the adih, beginning; ca, and ; he antah, end; ca eva, as also; the madhyam, middle-I am the origin, continuance and dissolution. At the commencement (verse 20) origin, end, etc. only of things possessed of souls were spoken of, but here the mention is of all creations in general. This is the difference. Vidyanam, among knowledges; I am the adhyatma-vidya, knowledge of the Self, it being the foremost because of its leading to liberation. Pravadatam, of those who date; aham, I; am vadah, Vada, which is preeminent since it is a means to determining true purport. Hence I am that . By the word pravadatam are here meant the different kinds of date held by dators, viz Vada, Jalpa, and Vitanda. [Vada: discussion with open-mindedness, with a veiw to determining true purport; jalpa: pointless date; Vitanda: wrangling discussion. [Jalpa is that mode of date by which both parties establish their own viewpoint through direct and indirect proofs, and refute the view of the opponent through circumvention (Chala) and false generalization (Jati) and by pointing out unfitness (of the opponent) tobe argued with (Nigraha-sthana). But where one party establishes his viewpoint, and the other refutes it through circumvention, false generalization and showing the unfitness of the opponent to be argued with, without establishing his own views, that is termed Vitanda. Jalpa and Vitanda result only in a trial of streangth between the opponents, who are both desirous of victory, But the result of Vada is the ascertainment of truth between the teacher and the disciple or between others, both unbiased.-Gloss of Sridhara Swami on this verse.]-Tr.]
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    10.32 Those that undergo creation are 'creatures'. Their beginning is the cause. The meaning is that, of the creatures which are being created at all times, I am Myself the creator. Similarly, I am the end, namely the destroyer of everyone of those who are being destroyed at all times. Similarly I am the middle, namely, the sustentation. The meaning is, I am the sustainer of those who are being sustained at all times. Of those who indulge in Jalpa (argument) and Vitanda (perverse criticism) etc., I am the fair reasoning which determines the truth.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    10.32 See Comment under 10.42
    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    10.32 Among creations I am the beginning, the middle and also the end, O Arjuna; among the sciences I am the science of the Self; and I am the logic among controversialists.
    Commentary

    10.32 सर्गाणाम् among creations? आदिः the beginning? अन्तः the end? च and? मध्यम् the middle? च and? एव also? अहम् I? अर्जुन O Arjuna? अध्यात्मविद्या the science of the Self? विद्यानाम् among sciences? वादः logic? प्रवदताम् among controversialists? अहम् I.Commentary I am the metaphysics among all sciences. I am knowledge of the Self among all branches of knowledge. I am the argument of dators. I am the logic of disputants. I am the speech of orators.In verse 20 above the Lord says? I am the beginning? the middle and the end of the whole movable and immovable creation. Here the whole creation in general is referred to.As the knowledge of the Self leads to the attainment of the final beatitude of life or salvation? it is the chief among all branches of knowledge.Pravadatam By the word controversialists? we should here understand the various kinds of people using various kinds of argumentation in logic such as Vada? Jalpa and Vitanda. Yada is a way of arguing by which one gets at the truth of a certain estion. The aspirants who are free from RagaDvesha and jealousy raise amongst themselves estions and answers and enter into discussions on philosophical problems in order to ascertain and understand the nature of the Truth. They do not argue in order to gain victory over one another. This is Vada. Jalpa is wrangling in which one asserts his own opinion and refutes that of his opponent. Vitanda is idle carping at the arguments of ones opponents. No attempt is made to establish the other side of the estion. In Jalpa and Vitanda one tries to defeat another. There is desire for victory.

    10.32 O Arjuna, of creations I am the beginning and the end as also the middle, I am the knowledge of the Self among knowledge; of those who date I am vada.

    Personal Guidance
    Of all creations, I am the beginning, the end, and the middle; of sciences, the science of the self; of debaters, the conclusive truth.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor self-knowledge (adhyātma-vidyā) as the highest science.
    • Aim for conclusive truth, not endless debate.
    • Use debate to arrive, not to wander.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I debate when I should conclude?
    • What conclusive truth have I been postponing?
    Analogy

    A great unrolled scroll has three places where a reader must pause — the beginning where it opens, the middle where the argument turns, the end where it concludes. Kṛṣṇa says of all creations: those three pause-points are Me. And of all the lessons such scrolls might teach, the science of the self is His own form. He picks the one knowledge that finally matters.

    Stories
    Kapila instructs Devahūti

    When Kardama Muni left for the forest, his wife Devahūti turned to their son Kapiladeva — the Lord Himself descended as her child — and begged for the knowledge that ends the cycle of birth and death.

    Kapila gave her the adhyātma-vidyā preserved in the Third Canto of the Bhāgavatam (SB 3.25–33): sāṅkhya not as dry enumeration but as bhakti-yoga, the jīva as eternal servant distinct from prakṛti and from Paramātmā, and devotional service to Bhagavān as the one science that frees the heart.

    Kṛṣṇa's claim here — 'of all knowledges I am adhyātma-vidyā' — is fulfilled in the form of Kapila Himself teaching it to His mother.

    Important Words
    • a - kāraḥ — the first letter A
      Compound: a (the vowel) + kāraḥ (the making, the syllable). The first phoneme of Sanskrit, the open vowel from which all other sounds derive. Kṛṣṇa picks the primordial sound itself, the seed of every alphabet.
    • dvandvaḥ — the dual
      Among Sanskrit's six samāsa-types (tatpuruṣa, dvandva, karmadhāraya, etc.), dvandva is the compound where both members retain equal status — neither subordinates the other. Kṛṣṇa picks the egalitarian form, perhaps as a hint about balanced relationships.
    • akṣayaḥ — eternal, inexhaustible
      From a (not) + kṣaya (decay). Modifying kālaḥ — distinguishes the infinite, dissolution-surviving time from ordinary measured time. Kṛṣṇa identifies with the kāla that does not itself end.
    • kālaḥ — time
      Time itself, qualified here by akṣayaḥ. The same kālaḥ that verse 30 named as 'subduer of subduers' returns here as Kṛṣṇa's own form — the great background measure of every existence.
    • dhātā — the creator
      From dhā — 'to place, establish.' The cosmic supporter and arranger. Kṛṣṇa identifies with the function of holding-together and bringing-forth, exercised in the universe through Brahmā but originating in Himself.
    • viśvataḥ - mukhaḥ — Brahmā, the four-headed one whose faces look in every direction
      Compound: viśvataḥ (in all directions) + mukha (face). Brahmā's epithet — his four faces survey the four quarters. Kṛṣṇa picks among creators the one whose vision is omnidirectional.
    Of letters I am the letter A, and among compound words I am the dual compound. I am also inexhaustible time, and of creators I am Brahmā.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    A among letters (its precondition), dvandva among compounds (its egalitarian pair-form), inexhaustible time, and the all-faced Creator. Kṛṣṇa names principles of speech, of duration, and of cosmic dispensation in one sweep.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The letter A is the inaudible base of every Sanskrit syllable. Choosing dvandva (which, in Pāṇini, allows constituents equal weight) is theologically charged: Kṛṣṇa identifies with the compound-type that does not subordinate one element to another. Akṣaya kāla and Dhātā (Brahmā with viśvato-mukha epithet, echoing Ṛgveda 10.81.3 to Viśvakarman) round out cosmic structure.

    Purport

    A-kāra, the first letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, is the beginning of the Vedic literature. Without a-kāra, nothing can be sounded; therefore it is the beginning of sound. In Sanskrit there are also many compound words, of which the dual word, like rāma-kṛṣṇa, is called dvandva. In this compound, the words rāma and kṛṣṇa have the same form, and therefore the compound is called dual. Among all kinds of killers, time is the ultimate because time kills everything. Time is the representative of Kṛṣṇa because in due course of time there will be a great fire and everything will be annihilated. Among the living entities who are creators, Brahmā, who has four heads, is the chief. Therefore he is a representative of the Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    33. I am the letter “a” among all letters. Among compounds, I am the dvandva. Among destroyers, I am Śiva and among creators, I am Brahmā, with four faces.
    Commentary

    The dvandva compound is superior among compounds since its elements are equal. [Note: In the avyayībhāva compound the first element is more important: adhyātma, in the soul. In the tat-puruṣa compound the second element is more important: guṇātita, surpassing the guṇas. In the bahu-vrīhi compound both elements are unimportant, depending on reference to a third element: mahā-bahuḥ, one who has strong arms.] Among destroyers I am indestructible time. This refers to Mahākāla, Rudra, famous as the destroyer. Among the creators I am Brahmā (dhātā), with four faces (viśvato mukhaḥ).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    33. I am the letter “a” among all letters. Among compounds, I am the dvandva. Among destroyers, I am the fire of universal destruction, and among creators, I am Brahma.
    Commentary

    Among the letters, I am “a.” The śruti says a-kāro vai sarvā vāk: the letter “a” is all letters. (Aitareya Āraṇyaka1.3.6) Among all types of compound words, I am the dvandva, because both elements have equal importance. In the other types of compounds avyayībhāva, tatpuruṣa, and bahuvrīhi one element is given more importance. Among the destroyers, I am the indestructible Kāla. This is the fire emanating from the mouth of Saṅkarṣana at the time of universal destruction. Among creators I am four-headed Brahmā (dhātā).

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In sanskrit no word can be pronounced without the vowel A. Similarly nothing can exist without Krsna. This 'compound word', according to Srila Jiva Goswami, in his grammar, is called the 'Rama‑Krsna' compound. It is when both parts are important. In other compounds, sometimes the first part is important but the second isn't or vice‑versa, or neither are important.

    Translation
    10.33 Of letters I am the alphabet 'a', which is the base of all letters as established in the Sruti: 'The letter 'a' itself is all speech' (Ai. Ai., 3.2.3). Samasika means collection of compound words. In it, I am the Dvandva compound; it is eminent because the meanings of both constituent terms are important. I am Myself imperishable Time composed of (divisions like) Kala, Muhurta etc. I am the four-faced Hiranyagarbha who is the creator of all.

    Personal Guidance
    Of letters I am the letter A; of compounds I am the dual; I am inexhaustible time; the creator with faces in all directions.
    Practical Applications
    • Treat sacred sound as His specific manifestation.
    • Read scripture aloud as participation in His sound-form.
    • Honor language itself.
    Reflection Questions
    • When did I last read scripture aloud?
    • What in language reveals Him?
    Analogy

    Of all letters, the first — the open mouth at the start of every syllable; of compounds, the dvandva that holds equals side by side; of time, the kind that cannot be exhausted; of creators, the highest. Kṛṣṇa picks the seeds: the first letter, the most balanced compound, the longest stretch of duration, the foundational maker.
